title: Andy Taylor Was Full of Surprises: Six Deep-Dive Career Moments
summary: Following his death at the age of 65, Billboard has highlighted some impressive, but overlooked moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.
content: Andy Taylor , the founding guitarist with Duran Duran , who passed away Monday (Nov. 23) following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, aged 65 , just might be the most underrated musician to emerge from the early 1980s. Taylor, who would also form The Power Station, enjoyed a solo career and was something of a serial collaborator, stood tall in a golden era for electric guitarists. Even the slickest commercial pop songs had destructive guitar solos, the type of which seem to be lost to this generation and last. Forget the Cold War, there was another arms race where the weapons of choice were plugged-in six-strings, with rows of effects pedals. Eddie Van Halen, Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, The Edge, Steve Stevens, Yngwie Malmsteen, Steve Lukather. It was an expansive group, and Andy Taylor was a member in good standing. Born in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in north east England, Taylor was the wild boy in Duran Duran – his autobiography from 2008 even carried that title. Here was a roguish rockstar with fast hands, itchy feet, who didn’t follow trends, but had many, many followers. But because of his breakthrough with Duran Duran, a band that drew a mystifying flood of hate from critics of the time, Taylor’s talents were largely overlooked. What he did next, couldn’t be ignored. Duran Duran split into two camps following the release of the 1985 James Bond hit “A View to a Kill.” Andy and John Taylor formed The Power Station, the funk-rock supergroup with Robert Palmer at the front, and Tony Thompson at the back, while Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor launched Arcadia, a collaborative-stacked project that, in an alternative universe, would’ve been Duran Duran’s fourth studio album. With The Power Station, Andy Taylor was unleashed. We got shredding, finger tapping, the works. Taylor contributed to the Duran Duran album from 1986, Notorious , then he was out. Fifteen years later, he returned to the band with original drummer Roger Taylor, to reunite the Fab Five. He contributed to the 2004 album Astronaut , and again on the 2023 collection Danse Macabre . The music world learned of his illness when, in 2022 , Duran Duran was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Taylor, his bandmates explained, as they read out a letter from the guitarist, was unable to attend due to illness. Billboard has compiled six deep-dive moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.

title: Inside the Madcap World of Chuyín: ‘Everyone Sings About the Neverending Party. I Sing About the Hangover’
summary: Meet Billboard ’s Latin Up-and-Comer Artist of the Month for November.
content: At the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards last month, a mob of Chuyíns in white straitjackets turned the stage into a psychiatric ward during a performance of “Pues Ya Ni Pedo.” The show’s closing gag revealed members of Fuerza Regida beneath the oversized masks — a fitting glimpse into the wonderfully chaotic world of the música mexicana breakout star’s May debut album, Los Locos Nunca Mueren (Crazy People Never Die). Related Who Is Chuyin? Masked Artist’s Debut Album ‘Los Locos Nunca Mueren’ Arrives on Billboard Charts Chuyin Unmasks First Billboard No. 1 With ‘Pues Qué Le Hago?’ All the Performances at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards But to understand the mysterious masked performer, first enter the void. “Before Chuyín, there was nothing, just black space,” the masked singer tells Billboard . According to his origin story, he came into existence on May 6, 2023, at a Fuerza Regida concert in Tepic, Nayarit, where frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz (JOP) “adopted” him. He’s been living with JOP ever since, he says, never once breaking character throughout the interview. Chuyín is three years old — or 21, if you count in dog years, as he does — and already making his mark on música mexicana. His 16-track debut album, released May 7 via Street Mob Records, debuted at No. 9 on the Top Regional Mexican Albums chart and No. 17 on Top Latin Albums , both dated May 23. In September, “Pues Qué Le Hago?” gave him his first No. 1 on a Billboard chart, topping Regional Mexican Airplay . On Los Locos Nunca Mueren , which features Fuerza Regida, Calle 24 , Luis R Conriquez , Óscar Maydon and Jorsshh, Chuyín takes on the carnal pleasures and intoxicating excesses common to contemporary corridos — then gives them a comedic twist. His protagonist doesn’t escape the consequences. On “Paniki,” a cheating Chuyín goes to ridiculous lengths to conceal his infidelity, only to get caught when he tries his luck again. On the album opener, “Rehabilitado,” he declares himself rehabilitated while remaining tempted by his vices. “Everyone sings about the never-ending party. I sing about the hangover,” he says. “Everyone sings about partying, partying and partying. I sang about getting sent to rehab.” Consequences are central to Chuyín’s character, but so is perseverance. “Chuyín is the guy everything happens to, and somehow he gets back up and keeps going,” he explains. “Everything that could go wrong happens to Chuyín, and he gets up with the same smile and says, ‘OK, let’s keep going.’” Behind the irreverence is an emotionally invested songwriter. Chuyín says he wrote “Olvídate de Mí” entirely on his own while living through the failed relationship that inspired it. Rather than admit that he’s the problem, he tells his partner to forget him — and run if she knows what’s good for her. The song reflects the openness he says defines the album. “If you listen to my music, you know me, and you don’t need to know anything else,” he says. “I give myself to the public completely, emotionally. And I think that’s what connected with people.” For Chuyín, concealing his face affords him the freedom to bare his soul. “I feel like I’m mysterious, but I’m very vulnerable in my music,” he says. “It’s a beautiful thing that people can get to know you without you showing your face, because of what you sing about. I always sing about personal things I’ve experienced.” With JOP as his mentor, Chuyín has honed his songwriting chops alongside Street Mob’s wider circle of creatives. “For me, writing music is like therapy,” he says. His songwriting extends beyond his own repertoire: He also helped pen Fuerza Regida’s “Tu Sancho.” Onstage, Chuyín has experienced both the scale of a Fuerza stadium show and the intimacy of his own performance. Singing with the group at Mexico City’s Estadio GNP Seguros in front of an estimated 80,000 people was exhilarating, he says. But a solo Chuyín show in Chicago, where 800 people had come specifically to see him, felt even more personal. “Both experiences were incredible, but they were very different,” he says. “Every one of those 800 people came just to see Chuyín.” Get to know Billboard ’s Latin Up-and-Comer Artist of the Month for November below. Name: Chuyín. Asked about the person behind the mask, he insists, “I’m Chuyín.” Age: 3 — or 21 in Chuyín years. Each year counts as seven because Chuyín is “like a little dog,” he says. Born and raised: Tepic, Nayarit, Mexico; Rancho Cucamonga, Calif. Recommended song: “Olvídate de Mí,” a candid account of romantic self-sabotage that Chuyín says he penned entirely on his own. Musical influences: His personal Mount Rushmore of música mexicana consists of Alfredo Olivas, Gerardo Ortiz, Natanael Cano and Junior H. Major accomplishment: Scoring his first Billboard No. 1 with “Pues Qué Le Hago?,” which topped Regional Mexican Airplay in September. “I put all the love in the world into the music,” he says. “The fact that the public embraced it and that I made it onto the Billboard charts is crazy.” What’s next: Chuyín is working on his sophomore album and exclusively reveals to Billboard that he will embark on his first headlining tour in 2027, with further details to be announced soon. The artist is preparing an immersive live show with one particularly mischievous tradition in mind: “At every show, I’m going to crown a Chuyín,” he says. “With every show, there will be one more Chuyín in this world.”

title: Was The Rolling Stones’ 1973 Still Part of the Band’s Classic Period, Or the Beginning of the End? (Greatest Pop Stars Podcast)
summary: This Vintage Pop Stardom episode of Greatest Pop Stars looks at a year where the World's Greatest Rock and Roll Band was at full power, but maybe moving into a different phase of its career.
content: In 1973, The Rolling Stones were coming off one of the greatest album runs in rock and roll history, a four-album stretch that cemented them as the World’s Greatest Rock and Roll Band, culminating in 1972’s Exile on Main Street and its legendarily hedonistic accompanying tour. Rather than take time off to victory lap following this iconic period, they headed to Jamaica to record their third album of the ’70s, released in 1973 as Goats Head Soup — which topped the Billboard 200 and spawned a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 single with breakup ballad “Angie,” but drew middling lukewarm and is now viewed by many fans as the beginning of the end of the band’s glory days. On this Vintage Pop Stardom episode of the Greatest Pop Stars podcast , host Andrew Unterberger is joined by Billboard executive digital director, east coast Joe Lynch — who wrote an excellent Stones cover story in July — to discuss a fascinating year in the Stones’ trajectory, where they were still one of the biggest bands in the world, but moving into their “holiday period” as rock standard-bearers. Along the way, we answer all the most pressing questions about the 1973 Rolling Stones: Was Goats Head Soup really that much of a step down for the Stones, or is it a bit misunderstood historically? Is it surprising we didn’t get more of a reggae album out of it? What was the deal with that album title and album cover? Is “Angie” a little too MOR for our tastes? How much did the band go on to miss Mick Taylor (and/or Jimmy Miller) after their departures? Was Truman Capote really unable to find a story following the Stones on their single most storied tour? And perhaps most importantly: Why the hell are we doing the 1973 Rolling Stones for this podcast right now anyway? Check it out above, along with a YouTube playlist of the Stones’ biggest 1973 moments — all of which are discussed in the episode — and subscribe to the Greatest Pop Stars podcast on Apple Music or Spotify (or wherever you get your podcasts ) for weekly discussions every Thursday about all things related to pop stardom! And as we say in every one of these GPS podcast posts — if you have the time and money to spare, please consider donating to any of these causes in the fight for trans rights: Transgender Law Center Trans Lifeline Destination Tomorrow Gender-Affirming Care Fundraising on GoFundMe Human Rights Campaign – In Your Area

title: ‘What A Talent’: Belinda Carlisle, UB40, Spandau Ballet & More Remember Andy Taylor
summary: Tributes are flooding in for Andy Taylor, the brawny founding guitarist for Duran Duran and The Power Station, who has passed away after a years-long battle with prostate cancer.
content: Tributes are flooding in for Andy Taylor , the brawny founding guitarist for Duran Duran and The Power Station, who has passed away after a years-long battle with prostate cancer. He was 65. “I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor – such a genius… he played the guitar solo in MAD ABOUT YOU, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” writes Belinda Carlisle on her social channels . “Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.” Legendary Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant joined Taylor on stage in Oxfordshire, England back in 2023, at a charity fundraiser gig for The Cancer Awareness Trust. “A tough fighter, Andy Taylor,” he recounts , “like so many…some of us get through…condolences to his tribe,” he writes. Fellow axeman Steve Stevens, the longtime talisman of Billy Idol, was heartbroken on the news. “F #ck cancer,” he writes . “Have so many memories with Andy. He was the first guitarist to sing my praises in the English press, I was forever grateful. He, Tony, & Robert are definitely jamming now,” says Stevens, a nod to the late Power Station members Tony Thompson and Robert Palmer. Duran Duran and Spandau Ballet were, for a time, the British second invasion’s pin-up boys. “Spandau Ballet are deeply saddened by the passing of Andy Taylor,” reads a message from the pop group . “Andy was a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene that we were all proud to be part of. Our thoughts are with his family, friends and fans around the world.” Spandau Ballet’s co-founder and songwriter Gary Kemp had his own words. “So sad to hear the news of Andy’s passing,” he writes. “A great player who set the tone for the eighties and influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style. He brought shameless rock to the mix. All my love to the Duran family. RIP Andy.” Like Duran Duran, UB40 for formed in Birmingham, England. “We have just heard the sad news that Andy Taylor, Duran Duran guitarist, has lost his long battle with Cancer,” a post reads . “Our thoughts are with his band mates and his family. Another one gone too soon! Big Love UB40.” Veteran British singer Michael Des Barres stepped up when Robert Palmer stepped out of The Power Station, the funk-rock band Andy and John Taylor formed in 1985 when Duran Duran was on hiatus. “He was a tough and rocking guitar player,” writes Des Barres . “He knew what he wanted, and he gave it to us. I was able to learn 22 songs in five days of rehearsal with the Power Station because of Andy‘s tremendous enthusiasm and professionalism. Simply put, he loved rock ‘n’ roll. RIP- My friend.” Terri Nunn’s Berlin paid tribute with a lyric to the band’s 1993 comeback classic “Ordinary World,” which featured Warren Cuccurullo on guitar. “Where is the life that I recognise? (Gone away) RIP #AndyTaylor.” The Dandy Warhols shared a picture of Courtney Taylor-Taylor i n his happy place , with a glass of red in his hand, and Andy Taylor at his side. Andy Taylor (no relation with John and Roger) had multiple stints in Duran Duran, scoring 13 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 , including two No. 1s: “The Reflex” in 1984 and “A View to a Kill” in 1985. The group’s beloved second album Rio album (which housed “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Save a Prayer,” and the title track) hit the Billboard 200 in 1982 and remained on the chart for a whopping 128 weeks. As a member of The Power Station, he earned three top 40 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1985, and as a soloist, he scored two entries on the chart: “Take It Easy” (No. 24 in 1986) and “When the Rain Comes Down” (No. 73 in 1986). Taylor was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022 in absentia due to his illness, which his bandmates announced from the platform of their induction speech for the very first time. It was the rocker’s former bandmates who shared the tragic news “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the group wrote on their website and on Instagram . “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.” The message continued, “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.” Also, Taylor’s wife, Tracey, shared a statement: “To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” she wrote. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” Andy is also survived by his children — Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew — and grandson Albie.

title: U2 Wind Back the Years With Classics, Dolly Parton Tribute for Thanksgiving Eve NFL Halftime Show
summary: The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix.
content: Cometh the hour, cometh U2 . The legendary Irish rock band, as they’ve done so often in the past, stepped into the cauldron, rocked out, and gave everyone what they were looking for. On this occasion, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. stepped into the colosseum that is the NFL’s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game at SoFi Stadium, pitting the Los Angeles Rams against the visiting Green Bay Packers. The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix. At the very top, the four bandmates took the long walk to the centerfield as a choir recited the lyrics of “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For.” “Thank you for having us,” Bono remarked over Mullen’s iconic, military-style drum pattern that launched the mini-set proper with “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” one of the band’s early political anthems. The production stepped up several gears as a marching band assembled and the song shapeshifted, interpolating The Supremes’ “Stop! In The Name of Love.” Then, a change in mood as U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton , the late queen of country’s smiling image splashed on three sails towering over the circular, center stage. Bono dueted with Dolly’s vocals for “Torn,” her very last recording which appears on the band’s 16th and latest studio album, Carnaval de Luz . And, in a moment that earned a roar from the audience, the band slotted seamlessly into another Joshua Tree number, “Where The Streets Have No Name.” The sails came down, and U2 got down to rockstar business — with some support from scores of backing singers. Without missing a beat, Bono and Co. reached into their glorybox with a rendition of “Pride (In The Name of Love)” a tribute to the assassinated civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., which appeared on their 1984 LP The Unforgettable Fire. And with that, U2 was done and it was game on. Carnaval de Luz this month debuted at No. 1 on three Billboard charts , including No. 1 on Top Rock Albums , Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales , and became the band’s 14th top 10 on the Billboard 200 (opening at No. 4). It’s their 12th No. 1 on the Official U.K. Albums Chart and Australia’s ARIA Chart. U2 this year chalks up its 50th anniversary, the celebrations for which will accelerate next year when the band returns to stadiums around the globe with Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show on Earth , its first stadium tour since 2019.
